definition: A single packet of electromagnetic radiation; its energy depends only on its frequency, $E = hf$, so higher-frequency light comes in more energetic photons.
The distance from one peak of a wave to the next, symbol $\lambda$; for electromagnetic radiation a longer wavelength means a lower frequency and less energy per photon.
A spectrum made of separate lines at only certain wavelengths, with gaps between them, instead of an unbroken band of colours.
The wavelengths of light given out by excited atoms as their electrons fall to lower energy levels; for a gaseous element it is a line spectrum that identifies the element.
An atom in which an electron has absorbed energy and moved up to a higher energy level than it occupies in the lowest-energy (ground) state.
One of the fixed energies an electron in an atom can have; the main energy levels are numbered $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ outwards from the nucleus, and level $n$ holds at most $2n^{2}$ electrons.
The way the lines in an emission spectrum get closer and closer together towards higher frequency (shorter wavelength), until they merge at a limit.
